title: Sugar paste rose
subtitle: Building a five-petal rose from gum paste or sugar paste from scratch
excerpt: A sugar paste rose is built petal by petal over a cone base, each petal thinned at the edge and cupped slightly before pressing to the cone. Gum paste sets harder and faster than sugar paste and is better for pieces that need to hold their shape without support.
sourceNotes: Sugar paste and gum paste flower-making is taught through the British Sugarcraft Guild and covered in decorating manuals produced from the 1970s onwards. Wilton Schools have published widely on the mechanics. The cone-base method is standard across British, American, and Australian sugarcraft traditions.

recipe.batchNotes: Make roses in batches and store in an open box at room temperature. They keep for several months once fully dry.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Roses must dry overnight before they are placed on a cake. Make at least 24 hours ahead.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pliable sugar-based paste stiffened with gum tragacanth or CMC (carboxymethyl cellulose) so it dries firm and holds fine detail. Stronger and faster-drying than sugar paste, and the standard choice for flowers and figurines.

A soft, pliable fondant-type paste used for covering cakes and modelling decorations. Less stiff than gum paste, it dries slowly and is better suited to flatter shapes that do not need to stand unsupported.

content.text: A sugar paste rose is a cone-and-petal construction. The central bud is a ball pressed onto a small cone; each subsequent petal is rolled thin and wrapped around the previous layer.
and is the better choice for anything that needs to stand upright. Work with small amounts at a time; both pastes skin and crack if left uncovered.
Roll a small ball of paste about the size of a marble. Pinch one end into a cone shape and press the flat base onto a piece of baking paper. This is your armature.

Roll a second ball roughly two-thirds the size. Press it flat between your fingers to a circle about 3 cm across, thinning the edge by pinching and turning. Press the thinned petal around the top of the cone, the edge just above the tip, and smooth the join closed with your fingertip.

Make three petals and attach them overlapping around the cone, each one tucked slightly under the edge of the previous. The inner petals sit close; the rose is still a tight bud at this stage. Curl the top edge of each petal outward very slightly between your finger and thumb.

The five outer petals are larger, rolled thinner at the edge, and opened out more before attaching. Space them evenly around the previous layer, pressing the base of each petal firmly to the cone and curling the edge back. A slight cup in the centre of each petal gives a more natural result. Leave to dry on baking paper before handling.

Roses need at least 8 hours to firm before they are safe to move and 24 hours before placement on a cake. Store uncovered in a cool dry place, not in an airtight box or a cold fridge, where condensation will melt the surface. Place on the finished cake with a dot of stiff royal icing.
Knead gel food colour into the paste a small amount at a time; it deepens as you work it in. Dust the finished rose with petal dust for a more natural finish once it is dry.
